paragraphs: As long as several men in assembly regard themselves as a single body, they have only a single will, which is concerned with their common preservation and general well-being. In such a case all the springs of the State are vigorous and simple, and its rules are clear and bright. There are no tangles or conflicts of interest. The common good is plainly visible everywhere, and only good sense is needed to see it. Peace, unity and equality are the enemies of political subtlety. Upright and simple men are hard to deceive precisely because they are simple. Traps and clever pretexts do not take them in, and they are not even subtle enough to be dupes. When we see bands of peasants, among the happiest people in the world, settling the affairs of State under an oak tree and always acting wisely, can we help despising the refined methods of other nations, which make themselves famous and wretched with so much art and mystery?

A State governed in this way needs very few laws. When it becomes necessary to issue new ones, everyone sees the necessity. The first man to propose them merely says what all have already felt. There is no need for factions, intrigues or eloquence to get passed into law what everyone has already resolved to do, as soon as he is sure the others will act with him.

Theorists go wrong because they see only States that were badly constituted from the beginning, and they are struck by the impossibility of applying such a policy to those. They have a good laugh over all the absurdities that a clever rascal or a smooth talker might get the people of Paris or London to believe. They do not know that the people of Berne would have put Cromwell to “the bells,” and the people of Geneva would have put the Duc de Beaufort on the treadmill.

But when the social bond begins to loosen and the State to grow weak, when particular interests begin to make themselves felt and smaller societies begin to influence the larger one, the common interest changes and finds opponents. Opinion is no longer unanimous. The general will ceases to be the will of all. Contradictory views and debates arise, and even the best advice is not accepted without dispute.

Finally, when the State is on the eve of ruin and keeps only a vain, illusory and formal existence, when the social bond is broken in every heart, and the meanest interest brazenly seizes the sacred name of “public good,” then the general will falls silent. All men, guided by secret motives, give their views as citizens no more than if the State had never existed, and unjust decrees aimed solely at private interest are passed under the name of laws.

Does it follow from this that the general will is destroyed or corrupted? Not at all. It is always constant, unalterable and pure, but it is subordinated to other wills that encroach on its territory. Each man, in detaching his interest from the common interest, sees clearly that he cannot separate them entirely. But his share in the public misfortunes seems negligible beside the exclusive good he aims to make his own. Apart from this particular good, he wills the general good in his own interest as strongly as anyone else. Even in selling his vote for money, he does not extinguish the general will in himself, but only evades it. His fault is to change the state of the question and to answer something other than what he is asked. Instead of saying by his vote, “It is to the advantage of the State,” he says, “It is to the advantage of this or that man or party that this or that view should prevail.” Thus the law of public order in assemblies is not so much to maintain the general will in them as to make sure that the question is always put to it, and the answer always given by it.

I could set down here many reflections on the simple right to vote in every act of sovereignty, a right no one can take from the citizens, and also on the right to state views, make proposals, divide the question and discuss it, which the government is always most careful to leave to its own members alone. But this important subject would need a treatise to itself, and it is impossible to say everything in a single work.
